scope: Public-source research reviews, adapted for public reading. Interpretations and proposed magnet research remain distinct from published findings. Private preparation context is omitted; no full reproduction was run.

reports.title: How representative studies are constructed
reports.title_zh: 代表研究的方法与证据边界
reports.body:
Steve Davis: how representative studies are constructed, and a feasible magnet-security contribution
Public-source methods review. Checked October 7, 2026.

The strongest contribution is a measurable extension from national trade exposure to delivered, qualified magnets. Davis’s published material-security work provides a useful baseline and demand scenarios; it does not establish the tentative hypothesis that mine diversification fails when downstream stages remain concentrated. That hypothesis should be tested in a model capable of finding either outcome.

Public code availability was inspected; no full reproduction was run. Availability does not establish that every dependency or result was reproduced.

Small study-method comparison

| Study | Actual study type and pipeline | Calibration/validation or sensitivity | Industry/experimental evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trade risks to energy security in net-zero emissions energy scenarios (2025) | National accounting/index + climate-energy and trade scenarios; imports, reserves, technology deployment and material requirements feed a trade-risk index. | Harmonized 2020 base year; Monte Carlo and alternative trade networks. Does not validate actual delivery disruptions. | No laboratory/field experiment; coauthors process several data sources. |
| Future demand for electricity generation materials under different climate mitigation scenarios (2023) | Exogenous IAM deployment paths × literature intensities, including replacement; material demand, embodied CO2 and production-growth comparisons. | Literature ranges, technology-share/lifetime/recycling sensitivities; historical production is a comparison benchmark. | No new mining or magnet-manufacturing experiment. |
| The importance of multiregional accounting for corporate carbon emissions (2025) | Matched single- versus multi-region environmentally extended input-output accounting, then company-revenue application. | Model checks against independent emissions statistics and country/industry data; sector imputation and industry averaging remain. | Watershed/CDP collaboration; commercial interests disclosed. |
| Food without agriculture (online 2023; issue 2024) | Literature-grounded engineering/life-cycle accounting of agricultural versus synthetic fats. | Energy/feedstock/land-use parameter grids; conditional system-boundary comparison. | Savor affiliation/equity disclosed; paper is not a new factory production trial. |
| Climate warming increases extreme daily wildfire growth risk in California (2023) | Observational fire-day prediction + climate counterfactual attribution, comparing neural networks, random forests and logistic models. | Held-out years, probability calibration/performance metrics and cool-to-warm extrapolation tests. | PG&E-supported weather-data processing and domain discussions; no randomized warming experiment. |
| Engineered bacterial siderophore production accelerates rock weathering for carbon removal (2026) | Mechanistic modeling + bacterial engineering/assays + pilot reactors + industrial-scale life-cycle analysis. | Measured dissolution/alkalinity and assay controls; process/LCA sensitivities. Industrial scale is modeled. | Actual wet-lab and pilot experiments; Davis’s stated role is advice on design/analysis. |

Table references: [Trade paper](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-025-02305-1), [Materials demand paper](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joule.2023.01.001), [Corporate accounting accepted manuscript](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-67759-5_reference.pdf), [Food paper](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41893-023-01241-2), [Wildfire paper](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06444-3), [Rock-weathering paper](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-026-03288-w).

The energy/material-security baseline in detail

The 2025 trade study covers 236 countries/regions, historical 1980–2020 and projections to 2060 using 1,092 AR6 scenarios reaching net-zero CO2 by 2060. For a commodity, TRI blends import-source concentration (HHI, sum of squared supplier shares), weighted by import fraction, with a reserve-based domestic dependency score weighted by domestic fraction. Aggregation uses energy/technology and commodity-value weights. The paper explicitly evaluates reserve-owning countries rather than current processing/manufacturing locations, arguing manufacturing can relocate faster than geology. It also acknowledges that fuel interruption affects operating infrastructure while material interruption can delay new construction; import economic value is a proxy for that distinction. These are exposure indices, not calibrated shortage probabilities. [Paper, Methods and Discussion](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02305-1).

The supplement makes the construction clearer. National scenarios exist for 74 countries (85% of population); others inherit regional changes applied to 2020 country baselines. Five-/ten-year scenario outputs are interpolated annually. Material demand follows new deployment, intensities, retirements and recycling. Trade networks are held fixed, expanded to reserve owners, or contracted. Sensitivity uses 5,000 triangular-distribution simulations each for energy systems, intensities and trading regions, plus 5,000 joint simulations; singleton intensity estimates stay fixed. Separate perturbations vary import fractions ±20%, recycling +0–20% and reserve quantities +0–20%. This quantifies assumption-driven variation, not observed disruption frequencies. Crucially, Table 8 maps Nd and Dy to UNCTAD “Ores and concentrates of base metals, n.e.s.” and GTAP “Mineral products nec,” with no direct UN Comtrade mapping. These are broad trade proxies, not measured NdFeB-grade oxide/metal/magnet flows. [Supplement, Table 8 and Text 1](https://media.springernature.com/original/springer-static/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41558-025-02305-1/MediaObjects/41558_2025_2305_MOESM1_ESM.pdf).

The public code archive has eight Python scripts, including data preparation, fuel/material TRI calculation and five plotting scripts. Inspection confirms a dependency score D=(1/236)^(e^2*r), where r is national share of global reserves. It expects absent mapping workbooks, preprocessed IEA data, reserve/production spreadsheets and trade inputs. There is no README or complete raw-input bundle. Its accessible snapshot is dated April 2024, preceding the final April 2025 publication; alignment with the final paper is unverified. The material script’s 0:14 selection also warrants clarification against the paper’s 16-material scope, rather than assuming a coding error. [Code archive](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8165867).

The Figshare archive contains 13 figure-source Excel files (five main, eight extended-data figures), useful for checking reported values/plots but not a full reconstruction from inputs. [Figure-source data, v1](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.28466435.v1).

Licensing affects exact reproduction: IEA World Energy Statistics and Balances is a subscription product; free highlights are narrower. The paper uses GTAP 11, whereas GTAP’s free historical archives currently extend through version 10. Do not assume that publicly described raw inputs mean a researcher can obtain the exact processed model. Public AR6 scenarios are available subject to their terms and registration/download process. [IEA product](https://www.iea.org/data-and-statistics/data-product/world-energy-statistics-balances), [GTAP 11](https://www.gtap.agecon.purdue.edu/databases/v11/), [Free GTAP archives](https://www.gtap.agecon.purdue.edu/databases/archives.asp), [AR6 v1.1 archive](https://zenodo.org/records/7197970).

The demand calculation is closer to a reproducible public starting point

The Joule study evaluates 15 materials under 75 climate-energy scenarios for 2020–2050. Comparing cumulative demand with geological reserves answers a different question from whether annual production, processing or qualified manufacturing can meet a deployment path. Its Nd/Dy result motivates production-growth scrutiny; it does not imply secure magnet deliveries. The full publisher article was not accessible in this review; the public archive was inspected directly. [Publisher abstract](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2542435123000016), [Author-institution summary](https://thebreakthrough.org/articles/future-demand-for-electricity-generation-materials-under-different-climate-mitigation-scenarios).

The 220-file archive includes corrected IAMC data, scenario lists, literature intensities with references, production/reserve/resource and carbon-intensity inputs, Python/notebooks, and outputs. Code calculates annual new build including lifetime-based replacement, multiplies by intensities, and runs 1,000 triangular intensity samples per scenario. Wind-generator shares are assumptions: baseline PMG shares rise offshore from 75% to 100%, onshore from 25% to 75% between 2020 and 2050; flat shares and 100% PMG are alternatives. Other sensitivities address thin-film solar, industrial decarbonization, recycling, lifetimes and emissions intensities. The README records manual correction of mislabeled onshore/offshore scenario fields and imputation of missing GCAM starting capacities. This demonstrates curation plus modeling, not merely applying a library. Hardcoded local paths and older pandas DataFrame.append usage require porting or a compatible environment. No full run was attempted. This is a demand postprocessor; supply shortages do not feed back into deployment. [Inputs, README, code and outputs](https://zenodo.org/records/7023703).

What the other studies add about research construction

Corporate accounting constructs a matched US single-region alternative to CEDA v5.0’s 148-region, 400-sector multi-region model. Leontief requirements propagate upstream production; emissions coefficients then produce factors. Detailed-country tables inform disaggregation of coarser tables; independent inventories and sector statistics provide checks. Application to 5,450 CDP-reporting firms’ revenues yields modeled accounting differences, not direct audits of physical underreporting. Industry-average factors, absent land-use-change emissions and scope-3 multiple counting limit interpretation. Davis is credited with co-conception, figures and writing; Andrew Dumit did input-output modeling. Watershed employment/equity is declared. [Accepted manuscript, Methods/contributions/interests](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-67759-5_reference.pdf).

The public corporate repo contains analytical/plotting scripts but imports an absent cliq package and requires CEDA/CDP inputs. The README explicitly requires CDP access; the paper states CDP data are licensed. Free Open CEDA factors do not supply the entire matched-model reconstruction or company microdata. The accessible code therefore supports inspection, not standalone exact reproduction from public inputs alone. [Repository](https://github.com/ProfFate/multiregional-acct), [Archived snapshot](https://zenodo.org/records/17355134), [Free CEDA factor product](https://openceda.org/solutions/ceda).

Food Without Agriculture is a useful example of Davis doing the analysis directly: author contributions credit him with the analytical approach and analyses. Its energy/GHG comparison varies feedstock, electricity and land-use accounting; chemically identical outputs do not eliminate upstream-system dependence. [Article](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41893-023-01241-2). MATLAB R2021b code and bundled .mat data are public; the code computes parameter surfaces rather than simulating a new production experiment. [Code/data](https://github.com/ProfFate/FoodWithoutAg).

Wildfire uses 17,910 observed fire-days (2003–2020), then alters climate-related predictors to construct a counterfactual. Davis’s contribution is schematic/communication/interpretation; Patrick Brown is credited with methodology and analysis. [Article](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06444-3). The supplement tests 1,000 neural-network configurations, 1,000 random forests and four logistic models, leaves three-year blocks out, uses log loss/Brier/reliability/ROC metrics, and tests training on cool versus testing on warm observations. This is stronger predictive validation than base-year harmonization, but a temperature counterfactual with other factors held fixed is not a complete future-fire forecast. [Supplement](https://media.springernature.com/original/springer-static/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41586-023-06444-3/MediaObjects/41586_2023_6444_MOESM1_ESM.pdf). Public MATLAB code exists; availability of the complete processed predictor dataset was not established. [Repository](https://github.com/ptbrown31/Climate-Driven-Risk-of-Extreme-Wildfire-in-California).

The August 2026 rock-weathering paper combines experiments with modeling: engineered bacteria, assay controls, dissolution measurements and pilot reactors with 4 kg substrate/11 L vessels support a mechanistic result. Gross removal and net removal differ: nutrients, rock preparation, electricity and inoculation enter life-cycle accounting. Industrial-scale extrapolation remains a model and sensitivities, not an operating commercial validation. Davis advised design/analysis; other named coauthors operated reactors and performed industrial modeling/LCA. [Article](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-026-03288-w). The collaborator’s public repository contains theoretical steady-state modeling and figure generation; reproducing biology/reactors needs materials, apparatus and experimental work beyond downloading code. [Mechanistic code](https://github.com/amoghpj/rock-weathering).

Recurring patterns — interpretation from the documented studies, not claims about daily routine

1. Define a decision-relevant system boundary and comparable output, then harmonize heterogeneous evidence into an accounting/modeling pipeline.
2. Link a technology or process to upstream requirements and broader system effects. A local advantage can depend on electricity, geography, feedstocks or supply organization.
3. Separate a baseline from counterfactuals/scenarios and expose assumptions with sensitivity tests. Different papers use different validation standards; “calibrated baseline” is not automatically predictive validation.
4. Divide work among modelers, data/domain experts and, in some papers, industry or experimental collaborators. Authorship contributions show that Davis’s role changes by project. Papers do not reveal his day-to-day coding/bench time or unpublished lab workflow.

AR6 ranges also need careful interpretation. IPCC describes its scenario database as an ensemble of opportunity; model/scenario counts are not draws from a calibrated probability distribution. Monte Carlo over assumed ranges likewise does not by itself supply real outage probabilities. [IPCC WGIII Chapter 3, scenario-database assessment](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-3/).

Publicly documented magnet-related scope and what remains unknown

The verified studies address Nd/Dy material demand and reserve/trade exposure. The lab’s current Materials/publication pages and public lab/personal repositories did not reveal a complete dedicated magnet-delivery project or stage-level dataset. This absence is not evidence that no project exists: the lab organization explicitly says repositories can remain private during preparation/review. [Materials research](https://sustainablesolutions.stanford.edu/research/materials/), [Publications](https://sustainablesolutions.stanford.edu/publications), [Lab GitHub](https://github.com/Sustainable-Solutions-Lab), [Davis GitHub](https://github.com/ProfFate).

Publicly reproducible work and additional evidence needed

| Work item | Publicly feasible now | Limitation/additional input |
|---|---|---|
| Trade-security baseline | Reimplement documented HHI/dependency formulas on a small, explicitly public dataset; inspect reported figure outputs. | Exact final-paper rerun needs correct snapshot, mappings and unavailable/licensed inputs. Call new-data implementation a replication of method, not identical result. |
| Generation-material demand | Port public demand code/input tables, inspect and reproduce selected Nd/Dy scenario/intensity calculations. | Runtime compatibility and path changes; verify chosen scenario/output checks before claiming full replication. |
| Stage-constrained magnet delivery | Construct transparent illustrative capacities, flows and shock scenarios from public evidence with ranges. | No verified comprehensive dataset for capacities, yields, usable inventories, customer-qualified suppliers, ramps or recovery. Public national trade proxies cannot fill all of these. |
| Factory-informed model improvement | Use manufacturing experience to define realistic questions and check assumed substitutability. | Quantitative private evidence is optional later; would need voluntarily available, appropriately shareable aggregated observations rather than assumed access. |

Five concrete research-design recommendations (proposed design, not Davis’s established findings)

1. Start with a small falsifiable question: for one specified NdFeB application/grade and customer region, compare delivered supply under a mine-only shock, a downstream-only shock and a correlated shock. State time resolution/horizon and usable form/quality at every stage. Keep “mine diversification helps” and “downstream bottlenecks dominate” as competing possibilities.

2. Build a minimal staged mass-balance model: mine concentrate → separated/refined oxides → metals/alloys → magnet manufacturing → qualified customer delivery. Represent stage capacity, yields, inventories, lead times and eligible supplier-to-customer links. These stages and parameters are a research proposal: specific recipes, material conversions and country/firm flows require verification. Begin with public bounds and explicitly illustrative values where evidence is missing. Preserve the published TRI as a comparator so the added stages’ effect can be measured.

3. Compare interventions under the same explicit budget and timing: additional mine sources, separation/refining capacity, magnet capacity, inventory, or qualification of alternative suppliers. Include recycling/substitution only with evidenced feasibility and timing. Use fill rate, cumulative unmet demand and time to restore a defined service level, alongside concentration. Costs and outage probabilities must be sourced or treated as ranges; with weak probabilities, compare robustness and break-even thresholds rather than invented expected losses.

4. Validate at two levels. Check conservation, units and baseline production/trade consistency; then, when observations exist, test predicted deliveries/recovery against a historical disruption with held-out periods or independent data. A fit to the same country trade inputs is not validation of shortages. If only public production/trade aggregates exist, state which delivery claims remain unvalidated.

5. Make uncertainty and data value part of the result. Vary correlated shocks, yields, capacity ramps, stock usability, demand/intensities and qualification delay. Identify when the recommended intervention changes. Anonymous expert ranges may help test pivotal assumptions without disclosing proprietary formulations, customer identities or supplier records.

Research-design questions

- Should a proposed magnet study focus on long-run material demand and trade exposure, or short-run delivery, inventories and recovery? Specify its application, geography and unit of analysis.
- Which published baseline could a staged delivery model extend, and what additional contribution would it test? Which assumption would manufacturing evidence most improve?
- Which archived code snapshot and mapping/input tables correspond to the final 2025 paper? What can a public-only partial replication establish?
- Which public evidence supports usable capacity, qualification, inventory and shock recovery? Which inputs are missing, and what validation is needed?
- What can a bounded pilot establish through baseline replication, one disruption case, or a parameter/data audit?

Exact reproduction is limited by licensed or missing inputs and code-snapshot alignment. These limitations should be documented rather than treated as resolved.

reports.title: Research evolution: the documented story
reports.body:
Steven J. Davis research evolution — public-source memo, verified 7 October 2026

Main interpretation: Davis's topics broaden, but the recurring construction is stable: start with a decision-relevant question; reveal consequences hidden by an accounting boundary or aggregate; quantify physical/technological constraints; then compare interventions. Magnets fit this pattern most convincingly as a testable constraint on delivered clean-energy technology, not only as a map of where rare-earth deposits or companies are located. This is an interpretation of the sources below, not a claim about an unpublished project.

TIMELINE

2008–2009: Early publications studied ancient western North American drainage, topography, and isotope paleohydrology. Examples are “The effect of drainage reorganization on paleoaltimetry studies” (2008) and “Synorogenic evolution of large-scale drainage patterns” (2009). The lab publications list verifies those dates and titles: https://sustainablesolutions.stanford.edu/publications .

2010: Two foundational questions emerge in parallel. “Consumption-based accounting of CO2 emissions” (online 8 March; issue 23 March) asks how the picture changes when emissions follow consumers rather than only the territory where fuel is burned; it estimated that 23% of 2004 global CO2 emissions were embodied in international trade. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20212122/ . “Future CO2 emissions and climate change from existing energy infrastructure” (10 September) asks how much future warming is already committed by installed devices, under assumptions about their continued operation and replacement. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20829483/ . Food/agricultural mitigation also appears in the 2010 publication record; breadth did not begin only recently.

2011: “The supply chain of CO2 emissions” follows the same carbon through fuel extraction, combustion, and final consumption. This changes the policy question from who appears to emit to where regulation can act efficiently. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3215011/ .

2014–2017: Trade accounting expands into air quality and human health. “China's international trade and air pollution in the United States” (online 21 January 2014) links economic/emissions accounting to atmospheric chemistry. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24449863/ . “Transboundary health impacts of transported global air pollution and international trade” (30 March 2017) combines four global models and distinguishes pollution physically transported across borders from pollution caused by producing goods for consumers elsewhere. https://www.nature.com/articles/nature21712 . The 2016 “Carbon Lock-In” review meanwhile broadens infrastructure inertia to interacting technological, institutional, and behavioral constraints. https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-environ-110615-085934 .

2016–2022: Structural materials become both an accounting problem and an intervention target. “Substantial global carbon uptake by cement carbonation” (2016) counts an overlooked carbon sink across cement's lifecycle. https://www.nature.com/articles/ngeo2840 . The materials publication record then includes cement/steel decarbonization and plant-level analysis in 2021–2023. https://sustainablesolutions.stanford.edu/research/materials/ . These are overlapping branches, not evidence that trade research was abandoned.

2018–2019: “Net-zero emissions energy systems” (29 June 2018) shifts from partial reductions to the complete system: reliable electricity, aviation, freight, steel and cement, and integration across industries. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29954954/ . “Geophysical constraints on the reliability of solar and wind power” (27 February 2018) tests weather variability rather than assuming annual energy balance means reliable supply. https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/2018/ee/c7ee03029k . The 1 July 2019 committed-emissions update finds existing/proposed infrastructure threatens the tighter 1.5°C budget, with explicit lifetime/utilization sensitivities. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1364-3 .

2020: Carbon Monitor converts heterogeneous activity data into daily, near-real-time emissions estimates, exposing temporal variation and the COVID shock/recovery that annual inventories obscure. The data descriptor was published 9 November 2020. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33168822/ .

2023: “Future demand for electricity generation materials under different climate mitigation scenarios” couples 75 climate-energy scenarios to material intensities through 2050. It finds cumulative generation-material demand below geological reserves, while production of Nd, Dy, tellurium, fiberglass and solar-grade polysilicon may have to expand considerably. This distinguishes having material in the ground from achieving an annual production flow. Scope is electricity-generation infrastructure; do not generalize it to every magnet end use. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2542435123000016 . Data/code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7023703 .

2025: “Trade risks to energy security in net-zero emissions energy scenarios” (9 April) links decarbonization, resource geography and trade: aggregate trade risk falls in 70% of countries, while electricity or transport risks rise in 82% of the countries becoming more dependent on imported materials. It tests trading networks, technology/material intensity and recycling assumptions. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-025-02305-1 . Code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8165867 . “The importance of multiregional accounting for corporate carbon emissions” was published online 20 December 2025, although the final journal volume is 2026. It brings the original boundary question to corporate Scope 3 inventories: geography can change estimated totals and mitigation/data-collection priorities. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-67759-5 .

2026: Continued focus on hidden deployment tradeoffs and consequences: a China solar study shows land costs alter tracking/fixed-tilt choices and thus panel/material requirements. https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2512930123 . A 30 June paper compares net-zero pathways with different carbon removal levels and finds different local health/equity outcomes despite the shared net-zero target. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-026-02675-0 . Stanford's 18 August AI seed-grant announcement lists Davis as co-PI, with PI Inês Azevedo and co-PIs Carlos Díaz-Marín and Edgar Virgüez, for a tool comparing US data-center locations/power strategies across costs, GHGs, resilience, air quality and reliability. https://bitsandwatts.stanford.edu/news/bits-watts-adds-eight-new-research-projects-its-sustainable-ai-infrastructure-research ; date verified from https://bitsandwatts.stanford.edu/events-news/news . Princeton's agenda lists his 1 October 2026 keynote “Contemplating the frontier of energy transition modeling”; it verifies the listing/title, not delivery or its content. https://acee.princeton.edu/2026-nzx-workshop/agenda/ .

DOCUMENTED REASONS VERSUS INTERPRETATIONS

Direct personal account: In Stanford's 27 September 2024 first-person profile, Davis says his paleohydrology results felt insufficiently relevant to decision makers. A student-founded product-carbon-footprint nonprofit introduced lifecycle analysis; meeting Ken Caldeira led to a postdoc proposal to account for all internationally traded goods. Davis says ideas also arise from reading, podcasts and conversation, with collaborators recruited when a question needs unfamiliar expertise. https://sustainability.stanford.edu/news/unraveling-ties-emissions-and-human-activities .

Direct explanation of the later intellectual shift: The abstract for his 3 November 2025 Stanford seminar “The Tough Stuff” describes the move, around 2018, from making emissions-reduction progress to reaching net zero as renewables became increasingly cost competitive. This motivated attention to the hardest-to-abate services and processes. This is his seminar's framing, not proof that all actual world renewable technologies had beaten fossil fuels everywhere. https://energy.stanford.edu/events/lecturepresentationtalk/stanford-energy-seminar-tough-stuff-steve-davis-earth-system-science .

Current lab explanation: The materials page says critical-mineral constraints become increasingly important as clean-energy construction accelerates. That directly supports a growing materials-security focus. It does not establish why any particular magnet project started, who requested it, or its unpublished scope. https://sustainablesolutions.stanford.edu/research/materials/ .

Interpretation: Accounting, lock-in, reliability and material security are connected by a repeated question: what does a headline target conceal about where impacts occur, when decisions matter, and which real-world constraint prevents the promised outcome? The 2025 corporate accounting paper also demonstrates that the earlier trade/accounting line remains active.

FIVE RECURRING RESEARCH HABITS

1. Start from a decision that would change if the answer were known. This is directly stated in the 2024 profile, rather than inferred from publication prestige.
2. Move the boundary until the missing consequence becomes visible: production to consumption (2010), extraction-to-consumption (2011), annual to daily emissions (2020), national to corporate/regional suppliers (2025).
3. Ask whether a scenario is physically and economically deliverable: weather/storage/reliable electricity (2018), annual material production (2023), land economics (2026). Often the operative constraint is more specific than the headline shortage or target.
4. Combine existing disciplinary tools around the question: economic accounting plus atmospheric/health models (2014/2017); energy scenarios plus material intensities/trade (2023/2025). His profile explicitly describes finding collaborators with needed expertise.
5. Turn uncertain assumptions into comparisons or sensitivities: infrastructure lifetime/utilization (2019), trade networks/material intensity/recycling (2025), low/high carbon removal (2026). The goal is often to show which intervention changes the ranking or outcome, not to predict one inevitable future.

PROPOSED MAGNET RESEARCH CONNECTIONS — NOT AN EXISTING DAVIS PROJECT DESCRIPTION

A strong candidate question: “How does resolving each manufacturing stage and specification-compatible magnet output change our estimate of clean-energy exposure to a supply disruption, and which intervention restores the most usable output for its cost and environmental impact?”

Begin by asking who is making the decision and what time horizon matters. A procurement decision, industrial investment, and long-run energy scenario require different measures. Possible outcomes include lost deployable MW or vehicles, months to recover usable supply, demand served, cost, or associated emissions. A national aggregate trade-risk index and a specific manufacturing bottleneck can both be informative; they answer different questions.

Manufacturing evidence could validate process yields and scrap routing, operating versus announced capacity, grade-to-application requirements, customer-qualified alternatives, and ramp-up or qualification times. These are candidate parameters to investigate; no proprietary factory data or unreported lab scope is asserted.

A bounded public-data study could combine a source-audited stage-by-stage dataset with a small model testing whether a manufacturing distinction reverses an intervention ranking. Scenario and sensitivity analysis should connect magnet requirements to deployment consequences.

RESEARCH-DESIGN QUESTIONS

1. “For a proposed magnet study, which decision would be improved, and should its core outcome be long-run trade exposure, near-term lost production, or recovery time?”
2. “The 2023 materials paper distinguishes geological availability from annual production needs, and the 2025 paper compares trade exposure. Would resolving NdFeB manufacturing stages, yields and specification-compatible capacity change an important conclusion, or is another missing constraint more valuable?”
3. “Which real-world assumption most affects an energy-transition model? What bounded manufacturing-evidence result would establish that resolving it changes a decision?”

EVIDENCE GAPS

- Public research pages are not a complete description of unpublished lab work. The 2025 study’s methods and supplementary evidence should be inspected before making claims about downstream coverage. Publication dates and author-contribution statements take precedence over bibliography annotations or author-order inference. A thematic interpretation does not establish private motives or a complete lab roadmap.
reports.basis: Completed timeline memo; distinguishes first-person explanations, publication history and interpretation.
